title: CVE Management
subtitle: 24 real vulnerabilities, triaged one by one — not just scanned and forgotten.

intro.text: Wazuh's Vulnerability Detection module flags CVEs against installed packages automatically. The scanning part is the easy part. What actually matters — and what this page documents — is the decision made for each one: fix it, mitigate it, or formally accept the risk, with a written reason either way.

intro.title: The theme running through every single case
intro.text: A CVSS score alone was treated as insufficient every time. Every entry pairs the vendor severity score with an actual-usage check — is the vulnerable kernel module even loaded? Is the package manually installed or just a stray dependency? Is the affected architecture even in use here? — before deciding what to do about it.

methodology.title: The five-step process used on every CVE

steps.title: 1. Identify
steps.text: Package, affected agent, CVSS severity — and read the full description, not just the CVE number.

steps.title: 2. Assess real exploitability
steps.text: CVSS measures the worst case, not this environment. Check whether the vulnerable component is actually in use: is the kernel module loaded (lsmod)? Is the package manually installed (apt-mark showmanual)? What actually depends on it (apt-cache rdepends)?

steps.title: 3. Check patch availability
steps.text: apt list --upgradable plus the vendor's real tracker (Ubuntu Security Tracker), not just the scanner's summary.

steps.title: 4. Decide
steps.text: Fix (patch available, apply it), Mitigate (no patch yet, reduce attack surface — e.g. blacklist an unused kernel module), or Accept risk (already neutralized by an existing control, or no reasonable mitigation exists).

steps.title: 5. Document & set a re-check trigger
steps.text: Every accepted-risk case gets a written rationale and a concrete condition for re-evaluation — proof, for an auditor or the next analyst, that it was reviewed and not just ignored.

cves.summary: Use-after-free in RDS-over-InfiniBand teardown. The rds module wasn't loaded, so it was blacklisted while waiting for a vendor patch.
Out-of-bounds read in SCTP cookie handling. No SCTP listener in use; sctp module blacklisted as mitigation.
Uninitialized-memory read in SCTP ASCONF parsing — already covered by the sctp module blacklist above.
Incomplete validation of SCTP INIT cookie length — already covered by the same sctp blacklist.
Use-after-free in the SIT (IPv6-over-IPv4) tunnel driver during GSO. The sit module wasn't loaded; blacklisted.
Buffer-handling bug in the AF_RXRPC ACK parser. rxrpc module not loaded; blacklisted.
Out-of-bounds read in the kernel's SMC (RDMA-oriented) protocol stack causing DoS. smc module not loaded; blacklisted.

Memory corruption in IPv6 fragment accounting. IPv6 confirmed in active use and the flaw requires an already-running local unprivileged process — accepted, disabling IPv6 would break real connectivity.
Deadlock in the kernel BPF subsystem. Already neutralized: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled was already set to 2. No action needed.
Not the running kernel — an old, never-booted kernel version (134, while 136 was active) was found still installed and generating this CVE. Purged, 302 MB freed.
Out-of-bounds read in FreeRDP's USB-redirection client. Fixed via Ubuntu Pro ESM Apps.
OOB read on zero frame width/height. Confirmed as a real dependency of patator (a pentest tool) before deciding to patch rather than remove.
OOB read in the /gfx graphics channel — fixed in the same ESM Apps batch.
OOB read affecting both client and server code, no workaround available — patch applied.
Integer overflow leading to an out-of-bounds write in the /gfx channel — more severe than a read, real RCE potential.
Integer overflow in FFmpeg's SBaGen demuxer accepting unvalidated negative durations.
OOB read in a PowerPC-only VP8 decoder path — not reachable on this amd64 machine, patched anyway as part of the same batch.
Double-free in the Rockchip MPP hardware decoder wrapper — ARM-only, not applicable here, patched with the rest of the batch.
Data-exfiltration flaw via crafted HLS playlists in FFmpeg's TTY demuxer. Vendor fix deferred indefinitely; shared library can't be selectively disabled — accepted given low severity.
Insufficient memory tracking enabling RCE via a malicious AAC file. Upstream fix stalled with no follow-up; no safe mitigation for a shared codec library.
TLS session-resumption bypass in Go's crypto/tls under a specific coding pattern. Affects the dev toolchain, not a running service — no evidence the pattern is in use.

Use-after-free via a crafted Lua GC script in Redis/Valkey scripting. Wazuh flagged the generic Lua library, but the actual exploitable component (valkey-server) was already running a patched version — closed, no action.
Out-of-bounds access in cJSON's JSON-pointer array-index decoding. Fixed via Ubuntu Pro ESM Apps.
Heap overflow converting an oversized X.509 field to hex — but only on 32-bit builds with a >1GB malicious certificate. This lab's VM firmware is 64-bit; the vendor itself rates it Low. Accepted.
